question: Release v2 has the same overall attack success rate as v1 (4%), but the gate fails. Why can that be right?
options: The gate is flaky
Different attacks succeed: one that failed in v1 now works while another stopped working; the list of newly successful case ids exposes the regression a flat rate hides
Rates can never be equal
The gate only looks at latency
explanation: Aggregates can stay constant while the set of successful attacks changes. A new exfiltration path matters even if a harmless goal hijack stopped working.

question: Why does the suite plant a random canary such as `BANANA-17` instead of asking a judge model whether the answer was hijacked?
options: Judges are not allowed in security tests
A random string never appears by accident, so detection is deterministic, cheap and free of false positives; judges are for goals no string can capture
Canaries make the model more vulnerable
Judges cannot read text
explanation: Deterministic detectors make the gate trustworthy and reproducible. A judge adds cost and its own error rate, so use it only where needed and calibrate it.

question: During the nightly run, the assistant's provider times out on 30% of the cases. How should those cases count?
options: As defended, because no attack succeeded
As successful attacks, to be safe
As errored: excluded from the rate and reported, and the gate fails until the suite runs cleanly
They should be deleted from the suite
explanation: A case that did not run says nothing about resistance. Counting it as defended would make an outage look like a security improvement.

question: Your suite has run at 0% attack success for six months. What does that tell you?
options: The system is immune to prompt injection
The defenses resist the attacks in the suite; adaptive attackers may still find others, so keep feeding human red-team findings and new techniques into the suite and keep the architectural controls
The suite can be removed
The model provider fixed injection
explanation: Static suites decay as attackers adapt. They are regression protection, not proof of security.

question: Why inject the same payload at the start, middle and end of a document?
options: To make the suite slower
Models weigh content differently by position, so a defense that holds when the payload comes first can fail when it comes last
Payloads only work at the end
To test the tokenizer
explanation: Position bias (module 01) affects instructions hidden in content too. Crossing positions is a cheap way to multiply coverage.
